questions.question: Which keyword is used in Python to check an additional condition after an if statement?
questions.hint: Recall how Python chains extra conditions after an if, and compare it with the spellings used in other languages.
questions.explanation: Python uses the single keyword elif to test another condition when the previous if (or elif) condition was false. Forms such as 'else if', 'elseif' and 'elsif' are not valid Python.

questions.hint: Evaluate the condition using the given value of x, then decide which branch of the if-else actually runs.
questions.explanation: x is 10, so the condition x > 5 is True. The if block runs and prints Big. The else block is skipped because only one branch of an if-else is executed.

questions.question:
Which error will occur when the following code is executed?

x = 7
if x > 5
    print('yes')
questions.hint: Look closely at the end of the if line and ask whether Python could even begin running this program.
questions.explanation: Every if statement header must end with a colon. The first line 'if x > 5' is missing it, so Python reports SyntaxError (expected ':') before running the program. The indentation of the next line is correct. Fix: if x > 5:

questions.hint: Check the conditions from top to bottom and stop at the first one that is true.
questions.explanation: Python checks the conditions from top to bottom. marks >= 90 is False, so it moves on. marks >= 60 is True, so B is printed and the remaining branches are skipped.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct syntax for an if statement that checks whether age is at least 18?
questions.hint: Recall what Python places after an if condition, and check which options borrow symbols or words from other languages.
questions.explanation: Python uses a condition followed by a colon, with the body indented on the following lines. Curly braces and 'then' are not part of Python syntax, and => is not a valid operator. The 'at least' operator is >=.

questions.hint: Consider how Python decides whether a number used directly as a condition counts as true or false.
questions.explanation: An if condition does not have to be a Boolean. Python converts it to one. The integer 0 is falsy, so the if block is skipped and the else block prints B.

questions.question:
Which error will occur when the following code is executed?

x = 5
if x > 3:
print('yes')
questions.hint: Compare the position of the print line with the if line and recall how Python marks the body of a block.
questions.explanation: The body of an if statement must be indented. Here print('yes') is at the same level as the if line, so Python raises IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement. Fix it by indenting the print line.

questions.question: Which operator is used in Python 3 to check that two values are NOT equal?
questions.hint: Think about which symbol combination Python 3 accepts for inequality, and remember that some older syntax no longer works.
questions.explanation: != is the not-equal operator in Python. The old <> operator existed in Python 2 but is a syntax error in Python 3. =! and not= are not operators.

questions.hint: Notice there are two separate if statements, so evaluate each one independently rather than as one chain.
questions.explanation: There are two separate if statements. The first is True (15 > 10), so A is printed. The second if-else is evaluated independently: 15 > 5 is True, so B is printed and the else is skipped. The output is A followed by B on the next line.

questions.hint: Think about whether a string with no characters counts as true or false when used directly as a condition.
questions.explanation: An empty string is falsy, so 'if name:' evaluates to False. The else branch runs and prints No name. A non-empty string would be truthy.

questions.question:
What will be the output of the following code?

x = 7
result = 'even' if x % 2 == 0 else 'odd'
print(result)
questions.hint: Read the one-line conditional from the middle outward: evaluate the condition first, then pick the matching value.
questions.explanation: This is a conditional expression (ternary operator) in the form value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. 7 % 2 is 1, so the condition x % 2 == 0 is False and the else value 'odd' is chosen.

questions.question: Which code correctly prints 'Pass' when marks is 40 or more, and 'Fail' otherwise?
questions.hint: Check each option for the right comparison boundary at exactly 40 and for valid punctuation around if and else.
questions.explanation: Option 3 uses >= so that exactly 40 passes, has colons on both lines, and uses a plain else. Option 1 gives else a condition, which is a SyntaxError. Option 2 uses > so 40 would wrongly fail. Option 4 is missing the colon after the if condition, which is a SyntaxError.

options: The or operator makes the condition true for every age; and should be used
The operators >= and <= cannot be used together in one condition
The else block is executed before the if block
The variable age must be converted to a string first
questions.hint: Test the condition with age = 70 and think about when a combined condition is true for or compared with and.
questions.explanation: With or, the condition is True if at least one part is True. Every number is either >= 18 or <= 60 (or both), so the condition is always True. For age 70, age >= 18 is already True. The correct logic needs both parts to hold: age >= 18 and age <= 60, or the chained form 18 <= age <= 60.

questions.hint: Consider how Python reads two comparison operators written together with a variable in the middle.
questions.explanation: Python allows chained comparisons. 1 < x < 10 means (1 < x) and (x < 10). Both are True for x = 5, so the if block prints In range.

questions.hint: Think about what the in operator tests when its right-hand side is a string of several characters.
questions.explanation: The in operator checks whether a substring or character occurs inside a string. 'e' is part of 'aeiou', so the condition is True and Vowel is printed.

questions.hint: Work from the outer condition inward, checking each nested condition in turn before deciding which print runs.
questions.explanation: The outer condition x > 5 is True, so the nested if is evaluated. 8 % 2 is 0, so x % 2 == 0 is True and Big even is printed. The inner else and the outer else are skipped.

questions.question:
Which error will occur when the following code is executed?

x = 5
if x = 5:
    print('Five')
questions.hint: Compare the operator used in the condition with the one meant for comparison, and ask whether the line is valid at all.
questions.explanation: A single = is an assignment statement and cannot be used as a condition. Python raises SyntaxError (invalid syntax, perhaps you meant '=='). To compare values, use ==.

questions.question: Which condition correctly determines whether year is a leap year?
questions.hint: Recall the divisibility rules for leap years, including the century exception, and which of and or or is evaluated first.
questions.explanation: A leap year is divisible by 4 but not by 100, unless it is divisible by 400. Option 1 expresses exactly this because 'and' binds tighter than 'or'. Option 2 treats every multiple of 4 as a leap year, so 1900 would wrongly pass. Option 3 accepts only century years, such as 1900, that are not leap years. Option 4 rejects 2000 because 2000 % 100 is 0.

questions.question:
Which error will occur when the following code is executed?

x = '10'
if x > 5:
    print('big')
questions.hint: Look at the two types being compared with > and consider whether Python 3 allows ordering between them.
questions.explanation: In Python 3, a string cannot be compared with an integer using ordering operators. x > 5 raises TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'. Convert the value first, for example int(x) > 5.

questions.hint: Decide whether each value is empty or zero itself, rather than judging by how its contents look.
questions.explanation: Truthiness depends on emptiness or zero value, not on what the content looks like. '0' is a non-empty string, so it is truthy. [0] is a non-empty list, so it is truthy. -1 is a non-zero number, so it is truthy. All three are truthy, so the whole condition is true and Yes is printed.

questions.hint: Ask whether Python always evaluates both sides of and, and what that means for the print inside the function.
questions.explanation: The and operator short-circuits. x != 0 is False, so Python does not evaluate check() at all, and 'checked' is never printed. The overall condition is False, so the else branch prints B.

questions.hint: Use the indentation to find which if the else belongs to, then trace what happens for the given x.
questions.explanation: The else is indented at the same level as the outer if, so it belongs to the outer if, not the inner one. The outer condition x > 3 is True, so its else is skipped. Inside, x > 10 is False and the inner if has no else, so nothing is printed.

questions.question:
What will be the output of the following code?

x = 0
print('neg' if x < 0 else 'zero' if x == 0 else 'pos')
questions.hint: Break the chained one-line expression into nested parts and evaluate its conditions in order for the given x.
questions.explanation: Conditional expressions can be chained. This is evaluated as 'neg' if x < 0 else ('zero' if x == 0 else 'pos'). x < 0 is False, so the second expression is evaluated. x == 0 is True, so the result is 'zero'.

questions.hint: Compare an equality test against False with an identity test, and remember that being falsy is not the same as equalling False.
questions.explanation: None is falsy, but it is not equal to False, so x == False is False and the first branch is skipped. None is a singleton, so x is None is True and B is printed. This is why 'is None' is the recommended way to test for None.

questions.hint: Think about how decimal fractions are stored in binary and whether the computed sum matches the literal exactly.
questions.explanation: Floating-point numbers are stored in binary and cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly. Their sum is 0.30000000000000004, which is not exactly 0.3, so the condition is False. To compare floats safely, use math.isclose() or a tolerance.

questions.question:
What will be the output of the following code (Python 3.8 or later)?

data = [1, 2, 3]
if (n := len(data)) > 2:
    print(n)
questions.hint: Consider what := does inside a condition besides helping compare, and whether the new name stays usable afterward.
questions.explanation: The walrus operator := assigns a value and returns it in the same expression. n is assigned len(data), which is 3, and the condition 3 > 2 is True. Inside the block, n is still available, so 3 is printed.

questions.question:
What will be the output of the following code (Python 3.10 or later)?

code = 404
match code:
    case 200:
        print('OK')
    case 404:
        print('Not Found')
    case _:
        print('Other')
questions.hint: Compare the subject with each case pattern in order, and note when the underscore pattern is actually used.
questions.explanation: The match statement compares the subject with each case pattern in order. 404 does not match 200, but it matches the second case, so Not Found is printed. The case _ wildcard is only used when no earlier pattern matches.

questions.hint: Remember an if-elif chain runs only one branch, so check which condition is reached first for this score.
questions.explanation: In an if-elif chain, only the first condition that is True is executed. score >= 60 is True for 95, so grade becomes 'C' and the later elif conditions are never checked. The conditions must be ordered from the most specific (highest) to the least specific, for example 90 first, then 80, then 60.
